title: Navi AI Companion Bot

heroImage.alt: Navi's animated virtual face displayed on screen
heroImage.caption: Navi's current animated face interface.

summary: Navi is an in-progress AI companion robot built around natural conversation, persistent memory, and an expressive animated face. The project currently combines a responsive visual interface, speech output, and an OpenAI-powered conversational brain with long-term memory.

sections.heading: The idea
paragraphs: Navi started as an experiment in building an AI companion that feels more like a persistent character than a traditional voice assistant. Instead of only responding to isolated prompts, Navi is designed to remember previous conversations, develop continuity over time, and communicate through both speech and an expressive animated face.

The long-term goal is to turn Navi into a self-contained physical companion robot. The project is still in active development, with the current focus on building and connecting the core software systems before completing the physical hardware.

sections.heading: Giving Navi a personality
paragraphs: Navi currently has a real-time animated face with responsive eyes and mouth movements, along with a synthesized voice for spoken responses. The visual interface is built to make conversations feel more expressive than interacting with a standard chatbot.

Her conversational system is connected to OpenAI and backed by a custom memory layer, allowing important details from previous conversations to persist rather than treating every interaction as completely new.

image.alt: Navi's animated eyes and mouth interface
image.caption: Navi's face is rendered in real time and designed to react during conversation.

sections.heading: Inside the build
paragraphs: Navi is built as a collection of independent systems for conversation, memory, speech, and animation. The conversational backend handles requests to the language model while a SQLite-based memory system stores selected information for future interactions.

Speech generation is handled locally using Piper TTS, while the interface uses Pyglet and ModernGL to render Navi's face. The project is being developed toward eventually running as a distributed system with a Jetson Xavier NX inside the physical robot and a more powerful computer handling heavier AI workloads.
Current development is focused on improving the conversation pipeline, memory behavior, speech recognition, facial responsiveness, and communication between Navi's hardware and AI services.

title: Pancake Test Fixture

heroImage.alt: Pancake manufacturing test interface with amplifier test results
heroImage.caption: The manufacturing test interface, built with Electron and Node.js showing a successful end-to-end test.

summary: A desktop interface for a bed of nails test fixture for SEA-310 amplifiers, collecting measurements, and diagnosing manufacturing faults.

sections.heading: Connecting software and hardware
paragraphs: For my senior design project at SDSU, my group created a bed of nails fixture to test SEA-310 amplifiers quickly, efficiently and easily. The test fixture utilizes a series of tests to search for manufacturing faults, record amplifier results for analysis, and produce performance metrics of the device under test (DUT) with a user-friendly interface.

The DUT connects to the Pancake test fixture through DUT test points that proxy signals to the Arduino using pogo pins and a ribbon cable. Measured outputs from the test fixture get relayed to 3 unique GUI pages for further analysis/debugging. I designed and programmed the software to interface with the Pancake test fixture.

image.alt: Amplifier circuit board mounted on the Pancake bed-of-nails test fixture
image.caption: This is our Pancake fixture with the PCB to test on top and our testing PCB and Arduino hidden underneath. The pogo pins allow us to measure at the test points.

sections.heading: My contribution
paragraphs: I was responsible for the software for my senior design group project at SDSU. I used Electron and Node.js to create the desktop GUI for the Pancake test fixture.
The interface used JSON and serial communication over USB to send commands to the Arduino and receive measurements from the fixture.
This data was collected, compiled, and compared against expected values as well as graphed for analysis.

sections.heading: The testing interface
paragraphs: A user may set each potentiometer (Drive, Tone, or Volume) to either CounterClockwise, Clockwise or Mid using the drop down menus on this screen. Presence is also set to ON or OFF using the last drop down menu. Finally, an amplitude and frequency can be specified. If there is an Arduino connected, the “Generate Signal” button will light green at which point the user may click it to send the command to the Arduino. If the command is successful, the GUI will display the signal information below the green button.

images.caption: A user can set the parameters on the GUI to configure the potentiometers, input level, and frequency at which to test. The results would be plotted on the shown graph and output to a .csv.

title: Basys3 Pinball

heroImage.alt: Basys3 FPGA board displaying a score beneath the virtual pinball game on a monitor
heroImage.caption: The pinball game running on a Basys3 FPGA and a VGA display.

summary: A simple virtual pinball game built in Verilog for a Basys3 FPGA, with scoring, flippers, sound, and a tilt mechanic.

sections.heading: From Pong to pinball
paragraphs: For my final project in CompE470L at SDSU, I created a pinball game using a Basys3, Verilog, a speaker, and a VGA cable. I experimented with “Pong” games people created online and eventually morphed it into my pinball game complete with scoring, flippers, a sound effect, tilting, and targets.

As I was creating the game, I found that there were situations in which the game could become slow or I felt that, as a user, I couldn’t manipulate the ball as much as I liked. Because of this, I added a moving target and the tilting capability. If you are familiar with physical pinball games, you’re aware that the ball can sink down the middle resulting in a lost ball regardless of how you use your flippers. To remedy this, pinball players will bump or “tilt” the machine to try to get the ball on a different trajectory. In the case of my game, a user can “tilt” causing the ball to switch its horizontal trajectory to the other direction.

image.alt: Block diagram connecting pinball logic, VGA sync, score display, clock, and buzzer modules
image.caption: The flashed code for verilog modules', inputs, and outputs as well as their bits are labeled.

sections.heading: Where it started
paragraphs: My inspiration for creating a virtual pinball came from my dad. He raised me a gamer and always encouraged me to play his arcade and pinball games.
